content: The recommended dosage of the medication is 2.5 grams administered intravenously every 6 hours for a duration of 4 to 14 days. The treatment duration depends on the severity of the condition, the location of the infection, and the patient’s clinical response. For patients under 18 years of age, the safety and efficacy of this medication have not been established. Since the drug is substantially excreted by the kidneys, patients with impaired renal function may have a higher risk of adverse reactions. Geriatric patients are more likely to have reduced renal function, so careful dose selection and monitoring of renal function are advised. Dosage adjustments are not required based on age but should be made according to renal function. Refer to adult dosing guidelines for further details. The combination of imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam can reduce the effectiveness of the BCG intravesical live vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. The prescribing information for intravesical BCG indicates that antimicrobial therapy for other infections may interfere with the vaccine’s effectiveness, particularly antibiotics active against mycobacteria. Avoiding all antimicrobial therapy during BCG treatment is currently recommended. This drug combination also reduces the effectiveness of the cholera vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Co-administration of systemic antibiotics with the cholera vaccine should be avoided, as these agents may act against the vaccine strain. The cholera vaccine should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam decreases the levels or effects of divalproex sodium through an unknown mechanism. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. In vitro and animal studies suggest that carbapenems may inhibit the hydrolysis of the valproic acid glucuronide metabolite back to valproic acid, thereby reducing serum concentrations of valproic acid/divalproex sodium. Co-administration of ganciclovir with imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam may increase the risk of seizures through an unknown mechanism. This combination should be avoided unless the potential benefit outweighs the risk. The drug combination reduces the effectiveness of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Oral microbiota products contain bacterial spores, and antibacterial agents may decrease their efficacy if co-administered. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Probenecid increases the levels of imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam by decreasing renal clearance. Co-administration increases the plasma levels and half-life of imipenem. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. The combination of imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam with valacyclovir may increase the risk of seizures through an unknown mechanism. Avoid this combination unless the potential benefit outweighs the risk. The drug combination reduces the effectiveness of sodium picosulfate by altering its metabolism. Co-administration with antibiotics decreases the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora needed to convert it to its active form. Use caution and monitor closely. Imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam reduces the effectiveness of live typhoid vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. It is recommended to postpone administering the vaccine until at least 3 days after completing the antibiotic regimen. Adverse effects of imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam include diarrhea (6%), nausea (6%), headache (4%), vomiting (3%), increased ALT or AST levels (3%), phlebitis or infusion site reactions (2%), fever (2%), hypertension (2%), anemia (1%), increased lipase levels (1%), central nervous system adverse effects (1%), and increased blood creatinine levels. Patients with a history of severe hypersensitivity to imipenem, cilastatin, relebactam, or any other component of the drug should not use this medication. Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in patients receiving beta-lactam therapy. A thorough allergy history should be assessed for previous hypersensitivity to carbapenems, penicillins, cephalosporins, other beta-lactams, and other allergens. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibacterial drug use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Prescribing antibiotics in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. There is insufficient data in pregnant women to determine whether there is a drug-associated risk for major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. There is also insufficient data on the presence of imipenem/cilastatin and relebactam in human milk, their effects on the breastfed child, or their effects on milk production. However, relebactam has been detected in the milk of lactating rats. The solution should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration before administration. It should appear colorless to yellow, and any discolored or particulate-containing solution should be discarded. Administer the drug intravenously over 30 minutes.
